title: The Guardian Legend

ines_header.note: Both figures check out against the file. 16 + 131072 = 131088, the size of the file, with nothing left over for CHR - and byte 5 asks for none. Unlike some dumps this header carries no anomaly that has been found so far; bytes 8-15 are all zero, so it is plain iNES rather than NES 2.0.

chr.evidence: iNES byte 5 is $00. By the iNES convention that means the cartridge has no CHR ROM and the board carries 8 KB of CHR RAM instead, which the file confirms by its size: header + PRG accounts for every one of the 131,088 bytes. NOT YET ESTABLISHED from the ROM: which code uploads the tiles. Per the playbook that is the whole graphics problem on a CHR RAM cartridge, and no uploader has been traced yet. The 8192 figure is the standard size for the board and is NOT derived from anything in this file.

mapper.name: UxROM
mapper.description: Mapper 2. A single write to any address in $8000-$FFFF loads the PRG bank register, which selects which 16 KB bank appears at $8000-$BFFF. The last bank - bank 7 here - is hard-wired at $C000-$FFFF and cannot be switched out, which is why the interrupt vectors and the switching code itself live there. There is no CHR banking, no scanline IRQ and no mapper-controlled mirroring: the board wires mirroring fixed, and iNES byte 6 bit 0 says vertical.

bus_conflicts.description: UxROM boards put the latch on the same bus as the ROM, so a write to $8000-$FFFF is ANDed with whatever the ROM already holds at that address unless the two agree. This ROM avoids that in the textbook way: it keeps a table of the eight bank values at $FFF2-$FFF9 and switches by reading a byte from the table and writing it straight back to the address it came from, so the written value and the ROM value are the same byte by construction.
bus_conflicts.evidence: $D79F-$D7A2 is LDA $FFF2,Y / STA $FFF2,Y, and $D70B-$D70E is the same pair. Seven more sites do it with a fixed address instead of an index - $D719/$D71C for bank 0, then $D726, $D733, $D740, $D74D, $D75A, $D767 for banks 1 to 6, each preceded by LDA #n / STA $04. A byte scan of the PRG for the three store opcodes based at $FFF2 (8D/9D/99) finds no other site.

mirroring.description: iNES byte 6 bit 0 is 1, which the specification reads as vertical mirroring. Mapper 2 has no mirroring control register, so unlike the MMC1 cartridges this toolchain came from, this cannot change at runtime and the header's bit is the whole answer. NOT CHECKED: whether the game ever relies on that arrangement in a way the ROM would show.

vectors.description: $DC75, $FEDE and $DCF3, all in bank 7 - which is the only place they could usefully be, since bank 7 is the one the CPU can always see. All three were disassembled and all three decode as the code their name implies: RESET is a textbook power-on sequence (SEI/CLD/LDX #$FF/TXS, then three PPUSTATUS polls, then a clear of $0000-$07FF), NMI saves A/X/Y and runs a vblank handler that does OAM DMA from page 2, and IRQ is a real handler rather than a bare RTI - it polls PPUSTATUS bit 6 and reloads DMC_FREQ. See the vectors region for the byte-level argument.

prg_banks.evidence: Opens with a 9-entry JMP table at $8000-$801A, then $FF fill. Nothing else in this bank has been traced.
Opens with a 5-entry JMP table at $8000-$800E. Nothing else in this bank has been traced.
Opens with a 12-entry JMP table at $8000-$8023. Nothing else in this bank has been traced.
Opens with a 10-entry JMP table at $8000-$801D. Nothing else in this bank has been traced.
Opens with a single JMP at $8000-$8002 and then falls into what decodes as code at $8003. The one-entry table is the odd one out among the eight banks and has not been explained.
Opens with a 20-entry JMP table at $8000-$803B, the largest of the switchable banks. Nothing else in this bank has been traced.
Opens with a 7-entry JMP table at $8000-$8014. Nothing else in this bank has been traced.

prg_banks.role: the fixed bank: vectors, bank switching, the far-call trampoline, the inline-argument helpers
prg_banks.evidence: UxROM wires the last bank to $C000-$FFFF permanently, and this is the last of the eight. Confirmed rather than assumed: the three interrupt vectors in this bank's own tail point at $DC75, $FEDE and $DCF3, and all three addresses decode as sensible handlers when this bank's bytes are placed at $C000. The seven fixed-address bank-switch routines at $D714-$D76E and the generic one at $D705 are also here, as they must be - code that switches the $8000 window cannot be running in the $8000 window. The boot-time bank check at $FF23-$FF43 selects each of the other seven banks in turn and confirms it answers with its own number, so the reset path itself asserts that this bank stays put while the others move.

open_threads: THE GRAPHICS, part done. The font is decoded and confirmed against a savestate - 45 glyphs, 1bpp, seven bytes each, bank 2 $8BF8, expanded by $806C. The BULK tile data is still not found; the savestate diff says 12.8% of live CHR appears verbatim in the ROM in codec-shaped literal runs. Next: find the decompressor, and take a second savestate from inside a stage.

Bank 4 is explained but still barely traced. It is 25 per-area screen-data blocks behind a pointer table at $8013, indexed by the area number in $51, and its single entry point returns a pointer rather than running code - which is why a control-flow trace found 19 bytes of it. The blocks are a command stream walked through ($BC) and dispatched by the 10-entry table at $E6F3, now resolved. Parsing the command stream would claim most of the bank; none of the ten handlers has been read yet.

RESOLVED, and stated here because the correction matters more than the finding: the two inline PPU-string routines were carried for a while as variable-length streams whose termination could not be established, on the reading that $D57C-$D584 loops over a run of items. It loops over ONE item, waiting for room - $D7C3 never touches $16/$17, so re-entering re-tests the same bytes. The block length is (first byte & $7F) + 3 for $D576 and two fewer for $D53F, and all 32 blocks the trace now reaches resume on a legal opcode. See annotations/dispatch.json and docs/text.html.

The game's text is decoded in all three of its formats: 32 inline PPU strings in the instruction stream, 20 dialogue messages behind a 21-entry pointer table at bank 5 $960F, and 3 screen scripts read by the renderer at bank 0 $8495. 3,056 bytes. docs/text.html lists all of it. The punctuation glyphs are read from context in every case and NONE can be settled from this ROM: a font would settle them and CHR is RAM, so no byte of the file is a tile until code uploads one.

A wording question raised from outside and settled against the bytes. A longer rendering of the corridor message was put to this project - 'THIS IS A MESSAGE SENT BY THE PREDECESSOR WHO INFILTRATED NAJU BEFORE YOU', 'MY HOME PLANET STAR NAU', 'I ESCAPED FROM NAU'. Its first and last paragraphs match this ROM's message almost verbatim; the middle does not. The words PREDECESSOR, INFILTRAT, ESCAPED, NAU, SEALS, OPERATIONS and MESSAGE SENT do not occur in this file in any case, under any of the 256 additive keys, any of the 256 XOR keys, bit reversal or nibble swapping. The only prose in the ROM is the bank 5 block. So the quoted wording is from a different source or revision, not something this search has failed to find - and that negative is a claim about exactly those searches.

What bit 7 of a PPU-string count byte means. Two sites use it - bank 0 $845F and $8469, both writing ':' and two spaces to PPU $2286 - and it is masked off before the length is computed, so the queue's consumer is what sees it.
The $C0-and-above form of a PPU-string item, whose length is a fixed 9 rather than a character count. Two sites, bank 5 $86DD and $86EE, and neither payload is ASCII.

26 reached routines never return - no RTS is reachable in any of them. That is computed by trace-code.py rather than listed, and it is what stops the walk at 5 call sites. The one that mattered: bank 2 $8AFF far-calls bank 0 $8015, an endless display loop, and the bytes after it are the block the pointer built at $8AC8/$8ACC names.

The three inline jump tables are read at one entry each, and that entry is never statically known, so in practice none is read at all: $9F2F and $A1C1 in bank 5 and $E6F0 in bank 7 all arrive with the index in A at runtime. Resolving them by hand into dispatch.json and seeding every entry is the next unlock after the strings. At $E6F0 ten plausible addresses follow the call, all $E7xx/$E8xx - but ten is where they stop at that one site and is not a claim about the others.

Bank 4 is reached at 20 bytes of 16,384. Its opening JMP table has a single entry, no far call in the ROM targets it, and no bank switch to 4 has been reached. Per playbook section 12, a bank that stalls this hard is one unenumerated mechanism, not a thousand separate problems.

JMP ($10C0) at bank 2 $8A97 is a jump through a RAM vector - $10C0 mirrors $00C0 in the 2 KB of CPU RAM. Nothing that installs it has been looked for. Playbook section 4 records this exact mechanism hiding a quarter of a bank on another cartridge.

The trace assumes a JSR returns with the live bank unchanged. 51 reached routines switch the bank in their own bodies and 89 call sites enter one; the list is computed by trace-code.py --risky and is untested rather than wrong, because a routine that switches and switches back is indistinguishable from one that does not without dataflow the tool does not do.

No latch write outside the nine switch routines is modelled. On UxROM any store into $8000-$FFFF loads the bank register, so a stray STA $8000 would switch banks. The check is an instruction-walk inventory of absolute stores over traced code; a byte scan is useless, as one run here confirmed by returning 1,331 distinct targets, nearly all operand bytes decoded as store opcodes.

CHR is RAM, so no tile exists in this file as a tile. No uploader has been found yet and no graphics region has been claimed. The cheap first question is not what points at a block but what routines write to $2007.

No reassembly check exists. Until one does, no claim about a region's extent has been machine-verified beyond its SHA-1 - and a SHA-1 says the bytes are the ones the writer meant, not that the boundaries are right. Build it before believing anything about extents.

The $FF runs at the end of each bank (37, 48, 16, 40, 14, 13, 46 bytes in banks 0-6 and 14 bytes at $FFE4 in bank 7) look like fill but are not claimed, because nothing has been checked about them beyond their byte value.
No RAM map exists yet. $04, $05, $10-$19, $21, $26, $2B, $2F, $30, $51, $54, $58-$5B, $76, $A5, $E4, $FC and $FE are all named by code read so far and have nowhere to be written down.
The routine the boot bank check calls on failure, $DED2, and the byte it stores at $0180, are not read - so what the seven failure codes at $FF3A mean is still open.

ppu_pipeline.summary: Every byte this ROM ever sends to the PPU goes through one write queue staged at $0100 in the stack page, drained in vblank by bank 7. The taxonomy is CLOSED: there are 31 STA $2007 sites and 18 STA $2006 sites in the whole file, all of them in bank 7, all of them traced.
ppu_pipeline.how_the_taxonomy_closes: An instruction walk over traced code found 31 PPUDATA writers and 18 PPUADDR writers. A byte scan of the WHOLE ROM for 8D 07 20 and 8D 06 20 found exactly the same 31 and 18 - so there is no PPU write hiding in untraced code. The scan also found one 8E 07 20 (STX $2007) at bank 0 $985C, and that is a false positive: it lies inside a descending 16-bit table, $07FE $078E $0720 $06BA $065A ... , whose differences fall smoothly. Indexed stores were checked too - four exist with a base that could reach $2007 given a large enough index, all based at $1F85 or $1FA9, which are RAM mirrors.
ppu_pipeline.entry_types: The queue entry is [count][ppu_hi][ppu_lo][data...]. The dispatcher at $DE15 reads the count byte and branches on its top two bits: below $80 is a run written with the PPU's increment of 1; $80-$BF is the same run with increment 32, set by ORA #$04 into PPUCTRL at $DEA2; $C0-$FF is an attribute-table read-modify-write, which reads VRAM twice and repeats until two reads agree. So the count byte is two fields in one, which is the idiom playbook section 5 names.
ppu_pipeline.producers: 24 call sites open a queue entry through $D6E0 (published as $C03C). The PPU high byte they write comes from $19 at 16 of them, from $AD, $18 or $03F8,Y at three more, and from an immediate at four: $2D, $27, $20 and $1F.
ppu_pipeline.chr_writes: The font is found and confirmed against hardware. Bank 2 $806C expands a 1bpp font stored at SEVEN bytes per glyph into 16-byte tiles - seven rows into the low bit plane, row 8 and the whole high plane zeroed - advancing the source by 7 and the destination by $10. Six records at $80EC drive it: 10 glyphs to $1300 (the digits at ASCII $30), 27 to $1400 (@ then A-Z at $40), and four single glyphs to $15B0, $15C0, $15D0 and $15E0. Expanding those 41 glyphs from the ROM and comparing them with the live CHR RAM of a title-screen savestate gives 41 of 41 exact. The other confirmed CHR write is the 5-byte status meter at PPU $1FF9 from $E3CC.
ppu_pipeline.not_established: The rest of the tile data. A savestate diff shows 1,046 of the 8,192 live CHR bytes present verbatim in the ROM across 13 stretches, whose sources march forward through bank 0 $8CDA-$9195 and bank 2 $93AE-$950E at a different rate from their destinations - which is what a codec's literal runs look like, and is a LEAD rather than a finding. No decompressor has been found, and there is not one STA (zp),Y among the traced instruction starts, so the whole class sits in untraced code. A second savestate from inside a stage would extend this: the same diff run against a different tileset would show whether the raw stretches move.
ppu_pipeline.searches_that_came_back_empty: Written down as claims about the searches, not about the ROM. (1) Rendering bank 1 and bank 6 as 2bpp tiles gives noise - no tile structure at all. (2) A scan for the 1bpp-font signature, sixteen or more consecutive tiles whose second bit plane is all zero, finds NOTHING anywhere in the file; on many cartridges that finds the font immediately. (3) Entropy per byte: banks 1, 2, 3 and 5 sit at 7.09 to 7.28, banks 0, 4, 6 and 7 at 6.49 to 6.93. Uncompressed NES tiles usually sit near 5 to 6.5, so the first four look compressed. (4) NO TRACED ROUTINE WRITES THROUGH A POINTER: there is not one STA (zp),Y among the 12,325 traced instruction starts. A byte scan finds 184 candidates in the whole ROM and none is at a traced instruction start. Since a decompressor almost always writes through a pointer, that puts the whole class in the 77 percent of the ROM the trace has not reached - which is consistent with a decompressor existing and with there being none, and distinguishes neither.
ppu_pipeline.what_would_settle_it: An FCEUX savestate. Playbook section 9 rates this the strongest check available because it is the hardware's own answer, and on a CHR RAM cartridge it is worth more than on any other kind: the savestate carries the live 8 KB of CHR RAM, which is the tile data itself. With that in hand the question stops being a search and becomes a comparison - if the tiles appear in the ROM the graphics are stored raw and the uploader can be found from the bytes, and if they do not appear anywhere the data is compressed and that is established rather than inferred from an entropy figure.
